claude.ai Chat

Here's What a Week Actually Looks Like
Every morning
"generate today" → daily digest built from all task files + calendar. 10 seconds.
After every meeting
Paste Granola notes → "process notes" → tasks proposed.
Every Friday, automated

Before any memo or presentation
Paste brief → "make slides" for HTML decks, or use Google MCP to generate and edit Docs and Sheets — with an outline approval step.
End of each session
"sync learnings" → context files updated with what Claude learned that session. Compounds over time.

MCPs Give Claude Hands — It Can Reach Into Live Systems
MCP = Model Context Protocol. Configure once, loads automatically every session.
  • G
    Google Workspace  Read/write Gmail, Calendar, Sheets, Drive, Docs. All three of my Google accounts — personal, Homage, CPOA.
  • #
    Slack  Send messages, look up channels and members, post digests. Resolves @handles automatically from a team member list.
  • Gr
    Granola  Pull structured meeting notes directly into workflows. "Process notes" triggers the full task classification flow — no copy-paste.
Without MCPs: Claude knows your files.   With MCPs: Claude can also act on your calendar, inbox, and Slack — in the same session.

10/24
CLAUDE.md: The File That Runs Before You Type Anything
"The difference between starting from zero and starting with full context — every session, automatically."
  • Context routing "If working on a Homage task, load business-profile.md. If personal, load personal-profile.md." I don't say this. CLAUDE.md says it.
  • Language + account routing CPOA work → Japanese automatically. Three Google accounts — CLAUDE.md picks the right one by task context.
  • Writing style Board deck → board style guide. Slack message → Slack tone rules. Product copy → product copy guide. Auto-loaded.
  • Skill routing A table mapping trigger phrases to skill files. "generate today" → today.md. "make slides" → slides/SKILL.md. Describe the task. Routing handles the rest.

The Folder Is the Database
  • CLAUDE.md Claude reads this first, every session. Routes everything else.
  • 00_context/ Everything Claude needs to know about my world. Profiles, style guides, org data, routing map.
  • 01_daily/tasks/ One file per task. The task database. Generates the daily digest.
  • 05_scripts/ Skill files (plain English) + automation scripts. Two distinct layers.
  • 02_projects/ Active projects with handoff sections for multi-session continuity.

00_context Is Claude's Knowledge Base — index.md Is the Map
How it works
  • index.md tells Claude which file to load based on what I'm working on. I describe the task. Routing happens automatically.
  • Slack aliases: org-data/slack_members.txt — every team member's display name. Claude writes messages with correct @handles automatically.
  • Stakeholder profiles: Short files on key people — role, what they own, what they care about. Claude loads the relevant one when drafting something sensitive.

13/24
One File Per Task. The Daily Note Builds Itself.
  • Structured task files Each file has frontmatter at the top: due date, status, owner, tags, project. Claude reads this block, not the prose below it.
  • Regeneration discipline Edit the source task file. Never manually edit the daily note — it regenerates from source files every morning. Manual edits disappear.
  • generate_today.py Reads all task files → builds daily digest sorted by project and priority. Runs in ~10 seconds. Opens in Obsidian.
  • Process-notes flow Paste a Granola meeting note → Claude proposes NEW / EDIT / DUPLICATE classification → you approve → task files created or updated.
  • Cross-device Daily note opens in Obsidian → same file synced to phone via iCloud. Same source, everywhere.

14/24
Skills vs Scripts: Two Layers That Do Different Jobs
Skill files (.md) — Instructions Claude follows
  • Plain English. Not code. You describe what to read, what to do, what to output.
  • Claude executes step by step when triggered by a phrase.
  • Nothing runs automatically — you trigger them in a session.
  • Examples: today.md, process-notes.md, slides/SKILL.md
Scripts (.py / .sh) — Automation that runs without Claude
  • Claude wrote these when I described what I needed. I reviewed and tested.
  • Run via macOS scheduler (launchd) — independent of whether any app is open.
  • Once tested, they run in the background without any session.
  • Examples: generate_today.py, au-digest-weekly.sh

Demo 1: A Day Starts With Two Commands
  • "generate today" Python script reads all task files → builds daily digest sorted by project and priority. 10 seconds. Opens in Obsidian. Same file on phone via iCloud.
  • "process notes" Paste Granola meeting notes → tasks proposed in under 60 seconds. Shows proposed text for each task before creating anything.
  • The approval table NEW / EDIT / DUPLICATE — Claude classifies, you decide. Nothing written without explicit approval. This is the pattern across the whole system.
Key rule: One task = one file. The daily note is generated, never manually maintained. Edit the source file — not the digest.

18/24
Demo 2: Automated Research That Applies Judgment, Not Just Aggregation
  • Source matrix 20+ companies, each with category, website, market context — defined once in markdown. This defines the research universe.
  • 8 research themes M&A, Regulatory, Product, Funding, Partnerships, Expansion, Talent, Customer Perception. Each maps to primary + secondary sources.
  • Quality bar built into the skill file "So what for Homage" is mandatory. Must lead with a competitive lever. Max 2 sentences. No generic "worth watching."
  • Three-layer automation Skill file (.md) defines quality → shell script (.sh) calls Claude + handles errors → launchd (.plist) schedules every Friday 8am. Independent of any open app.
  • Model: Haiku, not Opus Structured research tasks don't need the top model. Haiku runs the whole digest in under 3 minutes.

  • No external tools No PowerPoint. No Keynote. No design tool. No external libraries. Charts are inline SVG.

Five Moves for Five Situations
SituationMoveWhy it works
Same task, context still relevantContinueNo action — session context already loaded.
Wrong path taken/rewindErases failed attempt, rolls back file edits, keeps useful reads. Re-prompt with the lesson.
Session bloated with stale exploration/compact focus on X, drop YYou steer what's preserved. Claude compresses selectively.
Completely new task/clearFull reset. Fresh context window. Zero carryover noise.
Heavy subtask (research, doc scan)SubagentFresh Claude instance for one task. Result comes back as a clean summary. Your session stays small.

23/24
The People Who Never Hit Limits Think About How They Spend Tokens
1
New session per task
From ~message 30, Claude re-reads the full history on every turn. A simple question costs 50k+ tokens. /clear is the fix.
2
Group questions
One message with 3 sub-questions costs far less than 3 separate messages. Claude also produces better output — it sees the full goal.
3
Right model
Haiku for routine and research. Sonnet for most work. Opus only for genuinely complex tradeoffs.
4
Trim MCPs
Unused tools still consume context window space. Keep only what you actively use in current work.
5
Bite-sized files
This deck is built from small markdown files. Claude reads only what the task needs. File structure is token architecture.

24/24
You Don't Need the Full Stack. Start With One File.
Level 1 — 15 minutes
Create a CLAUDE.md
Your role, your team's priorities, 3 things Claude should always know. At session end: ask "what did you learn about my work today?" Copy the answer in.

Claude Desktop only. No VS Code needed.
Level 2 — 1 hour
Install Claude Code in VS Code
Add a context file for your main work area. Create one skill file for a recurring weekly workflow. Run it once manually and see what happens.

No automation needed yet.
Level 3 — Half day
Build a context library
3–5 context files + an index.md routing map + 2–3 skill files + daily digest. The system is live and compounding.

The one habit: ask Claude what it learned at end of every session. Save it. Repeat.
The habit that starts the compounding: ask Claude what it learned at the end of every session. Save the answer. Repeat.
